opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a bit of a shock at first, but in a good way. Before New York, most of my life had been in much more academic, fairly quiet environments, where your days revolve around the lab, the library, and a small circle of people doing similar research. Then you land in New York, and everything is just louder, faster, and more mixed together.

What struck me most was the density of different kinds of people. On one subway ride you might sit next to a finance person, an artist, a startup founder, a student, and someone who has lived in the same neighborhood for fifty years. In a research bubble you mostly talk to people who think like you. In New York you're constantly exposed to people with totally different priorities and ways of seeing the world, and that broadened my perspective quite a bit.

There's also a certain energy and directness. People are busy and ambitious, and they tell you what they think. At first that felt a little intense, but I came to appreciate it. It pushed me to be clearer about what I wanted and to move faster, which actually carried over into how I approach research and building systems.

And of course the food, the museums, just walking around different neighborhoods on a weekend. It was a nice reminder that there's a whole world outside of papers and deadlines. I think that balance was really healthy for me, and it shaped how I think about work and life even after I moved on.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing that hit me wasn't anything intellectual, it was the pace. In Beijing people move fast too, but New York has this particular energy where everyone on the sidewalk is on a mission, and nobody apologizes for it. I remember the first week I kept getting bumped by people on the subway stairs and thinking, is everyone angry at me? And then after about a month I was the one weaving around tourists.

The second thing was how much people talk. At Columbia, in seminars, in the hallway, at bars after talks, everyone is constantly pitching ideas, arguing, pushing back. Coming from a more reserved academic environment, that was uncomfortable at first. I'd sit in a reading group and someone would interrupt the speaker halfway through, and my instinct was that this was rude. It took me a while to understand that it's actually a form of respect, that engaging hard with someone's idea means you take it seriously.

And the third thing, which I think shaped me the most, was just how many different lives are packed into a few blocks. You could walk from a finance crowd in Midtown to artists in Bushwick to the Chinese community in Flushing in an afternoon. Nobody is the default. Being a foreigner in New York doesn't make you an outsider in the way it might somewhere else, because everyone is kind of an outsider. That was very freeing. I stopped worrying so much about whether my English was perfect or whether I fit in, because the city doesn't really ask you to fit in. It just asks you to show up and do something.

r001.rationale: The response describes feeling freer from pressure to fit in and worrying about English, but it does not say she felt free from being judged by others.

r002.rationale: The response says New York did not ask her to fit in; it does not state that she felt no need to judge others.

astra-6.text: What struck me was how many different worlds coexist in New York. You can walk from one neighborhood to another and hear different languages, see different kinds of art, and feel a completely different atmosphere. At first, that intensity can be overwhelming, but it also makes you curious. For me, experiencing the culture was less about visiting particular landmarks and more about walking around, watching people, and being open to something unfamiliar.
